title: NP-hardness of PosSLP
formal: Is \(\mathrm{PosSLP}\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Concretely, does there exist one deterministic Turing-computable map \(g\) and constants \(C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) such that \(g\) runs in time at most \(C(N+1)^d\) on every input of bit length \(N\), outputs a valid integer straight-line program, and for every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\), \[F\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{value}(g(F))>0?\] The reduction must be unconditionally correct on all inputs, with no algebraic conjecture, randomness, oracle or advice. Malformed input encodings are treated as no-instances and must also map to nonpositive outputs.

source_formulation.text: And finally, can we prove unconditional hardness results for PosSLP?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 14

why: A short sequence of elementary integer operations can represent numbers whose binary expansions are enormous. PosSLP isolates the task of deciding the sign of such a number. Its connections to numerical computation make a conventional hardness classification consequential well beyond the particular instruction format.
status_note: The checked 2024 primary papers leave unconditional PosSLP hardness open, and Miltzow’s March 2026 discussion still describes the NP-hardness evidence as conditional. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the specified deterministic many-one NP-hardness target. The source’s broader hardness direction is preserved separately and is not claimed equivalent to this concrete specialization.

progress.text: Bürgisser and Jindal publish their conditional randomized hardness implication and explicitly ask for unconditional NP-hardness in Section 6.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal publish results connecting integer sign testing to sums of squares, establish hardness for a polynomial variant, and retain unconditional PosSLP hardness as their final open question.
Miltzow posts an introduction to computation over the reals whose straight-line-program discussion still treats the NP-hardness evidence for PosSLP as conditional.

category_assignment.reason: The object is the exact sign of a succinctly computed integer.

importance.reason: PosSLP is a central bridge between exact arithmetic computation and discrete complexity, yet no general NP-hardness result is established in the checked literature. An unconditional reduction would materially clarify the computational strength of succinct integer sign testing and the interpretation of many PosSLP-hard numerical tasks.

sentences: The target is unconditional NP-hardness of deciding whether a succinctly represented integer is positive.
The integer is produced by a straight-line program starting from one and using only addition, subtraction and multiplication.
The required reduction must deterministically convert each 3-SAT instance to one such program in polynomial bit time.
Known conditional consequences for randomized algorithms and unconditional hardness of polynomial variants do not supply this reduction.
A complete answer would clarify the discrete complexity of exact sign testing without also requiring a proof that P and NP differ.

definitions: An integer straight-line program consists of an implicit initial value \(b_0=1\) and a finite sequence of \(m\ge0\) instructions. Instruction \(i\), for \(1\le i\le m\), is a triple \((j_i,k_i,\circ_i)\), where \(0\le j_i,k_i<i\) and \(\circ_i\in\{+,-,\times\}\); it defines \(b_i=b_{j_i}\circ_i b_{k_i}\). The output value is the exact integer \(b_m\), with output one when \(m=0\). Values may be negative or zero, and previous values may be reused arbitrarily. The program contains no input variables, divisions, roots, sign tests, branches, loops, separately supplied integer constants or compressed repetition instructions. The program is encoded by a self-delimited binary encoding of \(m\), followed in order by binary predecessor indices and an operation symbol for each instruction. All delimiters use a fixed finite alphabet; standard binary encodings of that alphabet are equivalent within constant factors. The PosSLP language accepts exactly valid encodings with positive output, and rejects valid zero or negative outputs and malformed programs. There is no promise on the sign or magnitude. A 3-CNF input is an explicit finite list of clauses, each containing at most three signed positive binary variable indices, with delimiters; repeated occurrences are allowed. Satisfiability means that some Boolean assignment to all occurring variables makes at least one literal in every clause true. An empty clause is false, and a conjunction with no clauses is true. The source input size \(N\) is its full encoded bit length. The reduction is one finite deterministic program on ordinary finite-alphabet Turing tapes; all reading, writing and index manipulation are charged by ordinary bit steps. Its time bound includes writing the entire straight-line program. It need not output the exponentially long binary expansion of the integer represented by that program. A many-one reduction makes one output instance with the displayed exact equivalence; it is not an adaptive oracle computation or a randomized transformation. Since 3-SAT is NP-complete under these reductions, this specific reduction is equivalent to NP-hardness, meaning that every language accepted by a polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machine has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to PosSLP.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must specify one reduction and prove its polynomial bit complexity, output validity and exact preservation of both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs. It must discharge every assumption needed for correctness. A negative answer must rule out all reductions of this form; failure of one construction does not suffice. NP-hardness is a relationship between decision problems and by itself does not establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), membership in NP, or NP-completeness of PosSLP. A conditional implication about randomized algorithms, an oracle reduction with no conversion to many-one form, or hardness for a polynomial-positivity variant does not meet this specified target.

context_blocks.text: The imported FSTTCS 2024 conclusion asks broadly for unconditional hardness results for PosSLP. To make that direction a single reviewable target, this card selects the concrete NP-hardness question explicitly posed in Bürgisser and Jindal’s earlier SODA 2024 conclusion, and fixes deterministic many-one reductions. It does not equate every possible hardness advance in the source direction with this particular target.

Bürgisser and Jindal show that a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for PosSLP would yield randomized polynomial-time algorithms for all NP languages, assuming an unproved constructive univariate-radical conjecture. This is a conditional complexity consequence and does not itself provide the unconditional deterministic reduction asked for here.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal prove unconditional coNP-hardness for a variant whose input represents a univariate polynomial and whose question is positivity at every real point. The quantification over real points changes the problem from testing the sign of one fixed integer. Their conclusion retains unconditional hardness of PosSLP as an open direction.

Miltzow’s March 2026 introduction to real computation again defines PosSLP by constant-one integer straight-line programs and describes the known NP-hardness results as conditional on assumptions that are far from resolved. Its informal discussion is used as a later status check; the complete input and reduction conventions here are stated independently.
